units.title: The KL-regularized objective and its optimal policy
outcomes: Derive the optimal completion distribution for a fixed reward and reference policy.
Explain how KL direction, reference support and the regularization coefficient constrain that solution.
units.why: DPO starts with a reward-maximization problem, not a classification trick. Its closed-form solution tells you which reference and support assumptions the later loss inherits.

next.note: Invert the optimal-policy expression and eliminate the partition function.

study.title: The RLHF Book: the optimal RLHF solution
study.locator: Chapter 8, DPO Derivation: Deriving the Optimal RLHF Solution (page read 2026-10-14)
study.depth: Stop before Deriving DPO Objectives for BT Models. Track maximizers, not equality of the objective values after sign changes and division by the regularization coefficient.

study.title: DPO: optimal-policy derivation
study.locator: arXiv:2305.18290v3, Section 3 equation 3, Section 4 equation 4 and Appendix A.1

focus: For each prompt, maximize expected reward minus \(\beta D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}})\), with \(\beta>0\). The expectation defining KL is under the policy being optimized.
The solution is \(\pi^*(y\mid x)=\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y\mid x)\exp(r(x,y)/\beta)/Z(x)\). Require a finite partition function and optimize on reference support.

Reuse Entropy, cross-entropy, KL divergence and mutual information and Constraints, KKT conditions and proximal methods. Here the new step is rewriting the reward objective as \(\beta\log Z(x)-\beta D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi\|\pi^*)\).
units.reproduce: Closed-book, derive the solution by normalization and certify it with the KL rewrite. For one prompt and two completions, take reference probabilities \((1/4,3/4)\), rewards \((\log 3,0)\) and \(\beta=1\). Obtain \(Z=3/2\), \(\pi^*=(1/2,1/2)\) and optimal objective \(\log(3/2)\). Check in CPU PyTorch with `torch.float64`, natural logs and absolute tolerance \(10^{-12}\); no sampling or model is needed.
traps: Reversing KL. A reference-to-policy penalty yields a different optimization problem.
Reading the penalty coefficient as a hard KL budget. A finite-data DPO run does not attain a prescribed divergence simply by setting it.
Giving positive mass to a completion with zero reference probability. Its policy-to-reference KL is infinite.

selfTest.q: Why does the partition function not change while optimizing the policy?
selfTest.a: The reward, reference and regularization coefficient are fixed. The partition function depends on these and the prompt, not on the candidate policy.

selfTest.q: What happens as the regularization coefficient grows without bound for bounded rewards?
selfTest.a: The exponential reward tilt approaches one, and the optimum approaches the reference distribution.

selfTest.q: Can a single sampled log-ratio be negative although KL is nonnegative?
selfTest.a: Yes. Nonnegativity holds for the expectation under the policy, not for each completion's log-ratio.

units.title: Implicit rewards from policy ratios and the DPO derivation
outcomes: Derive DPO by substituting policy-ratio rewards into a Bradley-Terry likelihood.
State the reward-identifiability, preference-model and coverage assumptions behind the substitution.
units.why: The partition function is intractable, but comparisons at the same prompt remove it. Knowing exactly why it cancels prevents using the derivation for mismatched prompts or treating finite-data fitting as an optimality guarantee.

next.note: Turn the likelihood into a stable tensor loss.

study.title: The RLHF Book: Bradley-Terry substitution
study.locator: Chapter 8, DPO Derivation: Deriving DPO Objectives for BT Models (page read 2026-10-14)
study.depth: Stop before Deriving the BT DPO Gradient.

study.title: DPO: reparameterization and reward equivalence
study.locator: arXiv:2305.18290v3, Section 4 equations 5 to 7, Section 5.1 Definition 1 and Lemmas 1 to 2, Appendix A.2

focus: Inversion gives \(r(x,y)=\beta\log(\pi^*(y\mid x)/\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y\mid x))+\beta\log Z(x)\). Keep the additive term until taking a same-prompt reward difference.
Bradley-Terry uses \(P(y_c\succ y_r\mid x)=\sigma(r(x,y_c)-r(x,y_r))\). Substitute first, then take the dataset mean negative log likelihood.

The implicit log-ratio reward is one representative of a prompt-dependent reward equivalence class. Fitting it needs preference coverage and a suitable policy family; the algebra alone supplies neither.
units.reproduce: Derive the likelihood and DPO loss without notes. Reuse the previous unit's two-completion setup: reference \((1/4,3/4)\), optimum \((1/2,1/2)\), \(\beta=1\). The two log-ratio rewards differ by \(\log 3\), so Bradley-Terry predicts preference probability \(3/4\). Add 7 to both original rewards and show that normalization, the optimal policy and the preference probability are unchanged.
traps: Dropping the partition term while claiming an absolute reward identity. It cancels in comparisons, not in the original reward equality.
Comparing completions from different prompts. Their partition constants need not agree.
Equating a finite empirical loss minimum with recovery of human preferences on unseen completions. The derivation is not a coverage or generalization theorem.

selfTest.q: Which reward transformations preserve the Bradley-Terry probabilities?
selfTest.a: Adding any function of the prompt to every completion reward. Multiplying rewards by a non-unit scale generally changes preference probabilities.

selfTest.q: Does the DPO derivation require training a separate reward network?
selfTest.a: No. It parameterizes the preference likelihood using policy-to-reference log ratios. The policy thereby supplies an implicit reward.

selfTest.q: Why is same-prompt cancellation insufficient to justify arbitrary preference labels?
selfTest.a: Cancellation is algebraic. The likelihood still assumes Bradley-Terry-style reward differences; contradictory, cyclic or population-mixed preferences may not admit that model.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: the DPO derivation in `policylab`, with a same-prompt reward-shift oracle and an explicit list of preference and reference assumptions.
units.stopWhen: You reconstruct the loss from the regularized objective, recover the three-quarter preference probability, and explain both the cancellation and its assumptions.

fit.note: The primary derivation and the paper's reward-equivalence result cover both topics at derive depth; the mini-project supplies the independent oracle.

units.title: Chosen and rejected log probabilities, reference log-ratio margins and the DPO loss
outcomes: Implement stable, pair-averaged DPO from four completion log-probability tensors.
Distinguish the raw policy gap, reference-adjusted margin and scaled reward margin.
Explain the regularization coefficient without assuming it fixes realized KL.
units.why: A plausible loss curve can hide a reversed reference ratio or the wrong reduction. A fixed log-probability example gives you an oracle before any language-model update.

next.note: Check update pressure and label order, not only the scalar loss.

study.title: The RLHF Book: DPO loss implementation
study.locator: Chapter 8, Implementation Details: log-probability gaps, `losses` and detached rewards (page read 2026-10-14)
study.depth: Use the code block. Do not adopt the following 'KL divergence is static' claim: finite gradient steps do not solve the objective exactly or set realized KL. Reference precomputation saves workload-dependent memory, not a guaranteed 50%.

study.title: DPO differential reference
study.locator: `DPOLoss.forward`: difference of log ratios, stable loss and pair mean

focus: Let \(m=(\ell_c-\ell_r)-(\ell_{\mathrm{ref},c}-\ell_{\mathrm{ref},r})\) and \(z=\beta m\). A pair contributes \(-\log\sigma(z)\); average over pairs, not completion tokens.
Use summed conditional completion log probabilities. The next unit checks gradient signs; Completion masks, length normalization and chat-template consistency checks how those sums are assembled.
Evaluate negative log-sigmoid directly, using `torch.nn.functional.logsigmoid`, rather than multiplying token probabilities or taking the log of an already saturated sigmoid.

For fixed rewards, larger \(\beta\) keeps the optimal policy closer to reference. In a fixed empirical DPO batch it also rescales logits and gradients; neither statement guarantees monotonic measured KL during training.
units.reproduce: On CPU, use PyTorch `torch.float64` leaf tensors for policy chosen and rejected log probabilities `[-1.0]` and `[-2.0]`, fixed reference tensors `[-1.5]` and `[-1.5]`, and \(\beta=0.5\). Derive \(m=1\), \(z=0.5\), chosen reward 0.25, rejected reward -0.25 and loss 0.4740769841801067. Implement the loss from blank tensors and match `DPOLoss` to absolute tolerance \(10^{-12}\). Repeat at logits -1000 and 1000 and require finite losses and gradients.
traps: Subtracting the chosen reference score but adding the rejected policy score. Write both chosen-minus-rejected gaps before subtracting the reference gap.
Detaching the policy log probabilities along with logging rewards. Only the logging path should lose its policy gradient.
Assuming positive adjusted margin means the chosen completion has greater raw probability. The reference gap can reverse the raw ordering.

selfTest.q: What is the loss when policy and reference score every completion identically?
selfTest.a: Each adjusted margin is zero, so each pair's loss is \(\log 2\), irrespective of its length or raw likelihood gap.

selfTest.q: Why not multiply token probabilities first?
selfTest.a: The product underflows for long sequences. Sum token log probabilities and keep the preference loss in a stable log-domain form.

selfTest.q: Does setting the regularization coefficient to zero recover SFT?
selfTest.a: No. DPO logits become zero, the loss is constant \(\log 2\), and its policy gradient vanishes.

units.title: DPO gradient weighting and chosen-rejected order invariants
outcomes: Derive the margin-dependent DPO gradient and verify it with autograd.
Test chosen-rejected swaps, label inversion and pair-order invariance.
Explain why hard or mislabeled pairs can dominate update pressure.
units.why: A correct scalar loss is not enough if labels, signs or gradients are wrong. These invariants isolate such failures without relying on a training curve.

next.note: Carry the verified gradient through the token-scoring path.

study.title: The RLHF Book: DPO gradient derivation
study.locator: Chapter 8, DPO Derivation: Deriving the BT DPO Gradient (page read 2026-10-14)

study.title: DPO: update weighting
study.locator: arXiv:2305.18290v3, Section 4, What does the DPO update do?

focus: For unscaled adjusted margin \(m\), \(\partial L/\partial m=-\beta\sigma(-\beta m)\). Thus the chosen and rejected log-probability partial derivatives have equal magnitudes and opposite signs.
Easy positive margins reduce this scalar weight. Hard negative margins increase it toward \(\beta\), including confidently contradicted labels that may be wrong.

Swapping chosen and rejected in both policy and reference negates \(z\). With a fixed winner label, \(L(-z)-L(z)=z\). Swapping candidate positions and inverting a binary target preserves binary cross-entropy.
These are partial derivatives of supplied log probabilities. Shared model parameters couple completions, so a parameter update need not increase every chosen completion's absolute probability.
units.reproduce: Derive the gradient closed-book. On CPU in PyTorch `torch.float64`, use unscaled margins `[-2.0, 0.0, 2.0]`, \(\beta=0.5\), and sum the three pair losses. The margin derivatives are approximately -0.36552928931500245, -0.25 and -0.13447071068499755. Match the analytic derivative with autograd and `torch.autograd.gradcheck`. For the preceding unit's single pair, recover chosen and rejected log-probability gradients -0.18877033439907273 and 0.18877033439907273, then verify swap and batch-permutation invariants to absolute tolerance \(10^{-12}\).
traps: Swapping only policy completions. Their reference scores must travel with their completion identities.
Checking the gradient of a mean against a derivative for a sum. A pair-averaged loss divides each pair contribution by batch size.
Calling gradient weighting a label-noise detector. A hard pair can be informative or mislabeled; its large weight does not distinguish those cases.

selfTest.q: At zero adjusted margin, what are the chosen and rejected partial derivatives?
selfTest.a: For one pair they are \(-\beta/2\) and \(+\beta/2\). Gradient descent therefore favors increasing the chosen-minus-rejected log-probability gap.

selfTest.q: Does a chosen-rejected swap preserve the loss?
selfTest.a: Not with a fixed winner target. It negates the logit and changes the loss by the original logit. Inverting the binary target as well preserves the represented comparison.

selfTest.q: Why might both completion probabilities fall even with correct gradient signs?
selfTest.a: The partial derivatives treat their log probabilities as separate inputs. A normalized model with shared parameters and other batch examples couples their changes and can move mass to other completions.

units.title: Completion masks, length normalization and chat-template consistency
outcomes: Implement shifted completion-only sequence scoring with explicit EOS and padding rules.
Demonstrate that replacing token sums with token means changes the preference objective.
Audit prompt-token identity, chat templates and truncation before comparing policy and reference scores.
units.why: DPO operates on conditional completion probabilities. Reuse The next-token objective: shifts, masks and perplexity and From documents to training examples: packing and loss masks; the new work is preserving that contract across four scores and two response lengths.

next.note: Bind each reference score to the exact tokenized completion.

study.title: Sequence scoring helper
study.locator: `compute_logprobs`: shifted logits, labels and mask; `average_log_prob` branches
study.depth: Pass a completion loss mask, not just the attention mask described in the docstring. Keep prompt tokens visible as context. Reject empty scored completions rather than letting the clamped mean denominator hide them.

study.title: TRL 1.15.0: data and preprocessing contract
study.locator: Expected dataset type and format; Preprocessing and tokenization; DPOConfig parameters `max_length` and `truncation_mode`
study.depth: Inspect the data contract only. Do not run the full quick start or assume its truncation matches the book's collator.

focus: For each completion, sum \(\log\pi(y_t\mid x,y_{<t})\) over scored target positions. Shift the completion mask with the labels exactly once.

A common prompt's joint log probability cancels algebraically in a same-prompt difference. Different templates, token boundaries or per-response prompt truncation invalidate that argument; compare actual prompt token IDs.
Token means are not sequence log probabilities. Unequal lengths change the adjusted margin and the gradient weighting, even when both policy and reference are normalized consistently.

Declare whether EOS is scored, where completion starts, how padding is excluded and what overlength pairs lose. Inspect rendered text and token IDs for both branches; do not silently train after truncation removes the preferred distinction.
units.reproduce: On CPU with PyTorch `torch.float64`, use zero logits of shape `(1, 4, 2)`, token IDs `[[0, 1, 0, 1]]` and an unshifted completion mask `[[0, 0, 1, 1]]`. Derive the shifted selected targets, score \(-2\log 2\), and mean \(-\log 2\). Match `compute_logprobs` to absolute tolerance \(10^{-12}\). Only scoring-logit positions 1 and 2 receive gradients. Give the rejected branch one scored token: with identical policy and reference, adjusted margin stays zero although the raw policy gap is \(-\log 2\). Then test an actual template's completion boundary and an overlength pair in your scorer.
traps: Removing prompt tokens from attention to achieve completion-only loss. They remain necessary conditioning context.
Masking by token ID when padding reuses EOS. That can remove real EOS targets; mask by position and sequence ownership instead.
Comparing separately tokenized prompt lengths without checking the full sequence prefix. Tokenization at a text boundary can change IDs.

selfTest.q: Can changing prompt input tokens change a completion-only loss?
selfTest.a: Yes. Prompt targets are excluded, but prompt inputs still condition completion predictions. Only excluded scoring logits can be perturbed independently without affecting the score.

selfTest.q: Why does replacing sums by means not simply rescale the whole batch?
selfTest.a: Chosen and rejected lengths can differ within a pair and across pairs. Each score then gets a different divisor.

selfTest.q: What should happen if truncation leaves no scored completion tokens?
selfTest.a: Reject or explicitly classify the record as invalid and count it. A zero sum or clamped denominator is not a meaningful preference example.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: `policylab` completion-scoring oracles for shifts, unequal lengths, EOS-as-padding, templates, empty responses and truncation, with token-level evidence for each policy-reference pair.
units.stopWhen: Your scorer passes the fixed-logit oracle and boundary tests, and you can exhibit an unequal-length pair whose adjusted margin changes under token means.

fit.note: The scoring helper, versioned trainer contract and SimPO score definition cover masks, lengths and templates; mini-project boundary tests provide implementation practice.

units.title: Reference identity and drift, and preference-data support mismatch
outcomes: Explain why a frozen reference checkpoint and reproducible score provenance define the DPO objective.
Distinguish zero reference support from poor practical coverage in an offline preference dataset.
Explain why data generated by another policy can leave deployment behavior unconstrained.
units.why: The reference is part of the objective, not just an extra model in memory. Meanwhile, nonzero token probabilities do not mean the preference dataset covers what the trained policy will generate.

next.note: Separate objective choice from how and when comparisons were collected.

study.title: The RLHF Book: policy-dependent preference data
study.locator: Chapter 8, DAAs with Synthetic Preference Data (page read 2026-10-14)
study.depth: Read the contrast between matching the generating policy and learning from chosen-rejected differences. Treat these as empirical data-design findings, not a theorem that one collection policy always wins.

study.title: DPO: reference initialization and support
study.locator: arXiv:2305.18290v3, Section 4, DPO outline; Appendix A.6, full-support assumption in the proof of Theorem 1

focus: Bind reference scores to checkpoint or adapter identity, tokenizer, template, exact token IDs, completion mask and truncation rule. A score keyed only by prompt text is insufficient.
Keep reference parameters outside the optimizer and score deterministically. Precomputed scores remain valid only while both reference identity and preprocessing stay fixed.

With \(\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y\mid x)=0\), a positive policy probability gives infinite policy-to-reference KL. With a full-softmax model, the common problem is instead tiny probability and absent or unrepresentative comparisons.

Audit generating-policy and annotator provenance, prompt families and chosen-rejected likelihood and length distributions. A rising margin on collected pairs does not constrain all unobserved responses.
units.reproduce: Draw the provenance chain for one preference pair and explain which artifacts invalidate precomputed scores. Use policy log probabilities -1 and -2, reference log probabilities -1.5 and -1.5, and \(\beta=0.5\). Changing only the reference scores to -1 and -2 moves the loss from 0.4740769841801067 to \(\log 2\) although the policy did not change. Explain why replacing the reference by a freshly detached copy of the policy resets margins but does not make policy gradients vanish.
traps: Calling a reference frozen because its outputs are detached. Its parameters or adapters can still drift if shared with the policy or updated elsewhere.
Confusing reference support with dataset support. Full token support does not supply missing comparisons.
Enabling `sync_ref_model=True` while describing the experiment as fixed-reference DPO. Reference synchronization changes the training procedure.

selfTest.q: Does reusing cached scores survive a changed chat template?
selfTest.a: Not automatically. The tokenized event or context may change. Recompute after verifying the new input and mask identities.

selfTest.q: Why can two identical checkpoints produce nonzero measured margins at initialization?
selfTest.a: Stochastic scoring, differing precision or preprocessing can produce different scores. Disable stochastic layers and compare identical tokenized inputs before attributing the difference to learning.

selfTest.q: Must all preference responses come from the reference policy?
selfTest.a: No. The finite-data likelihood can be evaluated on other policies' responses where scores exist. Its usefulness still depends on coverage, labels and generalization to the policy's generated responses.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: a reference-score manifest, a deliberate reference-drift failure and a preference-data support audit in `policylab`.
units.stopWhen: You explain the reference-only loss change, identify every score-invalidating artifact and distinguish formal support failure from missing preference coverage.

fit.note: The book's data discussion, the paper's reference assumptions and versioned TRL options cover both explain targets; the mini-project supplies provenance and drift practice.
